claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the capacity to form and maintain an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer together with a robust passive oxide film.
An ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer can reduce friction and wear in a high-entropy alloy.
The combination of a refined surface layer and a passive oxide film minimizes both abrasive wear and corrosive degradation.
B microalloying promotes in situ precipitation of fine reinforcing phases.
Controlled sliding or high surface shear can induce near-surface grain refinement and local amorphization.
An ultra-fine or amorphous near-surface layer supports rapid in situ development of a protective passive oxide film.
The passive oxide film supported by the refined surface layer is self-healing after mechanical disruption.
Mo and possible B additions promote formation of a chemically stable passive layer under tribocorrosion.
Rapid healing of disrupted passivation diminishes both abrasive wear and corrosion.
A refined or amorphous surface will produce a lower wear rate than a conventionally coarse matched baseline.
A refined or amorphous surface will produce a lower corrosion current density than the matched baseline.
A refined or amorphous surface will produce smaller open-circuit-potential shifts during tribocorrosion than the matched baseline.
The modified alloy will exhibit significantly better combined tribocorrosion performance than the baseline.
The improved combined performance results from synergy between mechanical accommodation by the refined layer and chemical passivation.
The protective benefit should hold at moderate temperatures and strain rates where the passive film remains stable.
The protective benefit may fail at extreme temperatures or very high strain rates when passive-film disruption outpaces repair.
The critical grain size or amorphous fraction required for optimal protection is not quantitatively established.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in wear rate and corrosion current density and improved OCP stability would falsify the predicted performance.
Failure to observe a dynamically refined or amorphous passivating layer would falsify the proposed mechanism.
